rows.title: Synapsis — the framework of NuclearLang — Rules
rows.summary: 1. A platform is what is written; a dialect is only how it comes out.
body: 1. **A platform is what is written; a dialect is only how it comes out.** Kinds, decorators, folders,
`config.nuc`, plugins and tests are the platform's, in Nuclear, the same for every dialect of it. Kinds and
features may differ between platforms, never between the dialects of one platform.
2. **The one exception** is code that uses a dialect's type definitions (`numpy` exists only in Python), or a kind
package implemented for some dialects: allowed, and it ties that project to those dialects.
3. **A platform names no dialect and no target's library.** Its contract, reference, docs, examples and
diagnostics hold only Nuclear and Nuclear's own library (`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/library.md`).
4. **Kinds are data, never compiler code:** TOML, templates, a runtime package and docs. What a template cannot
express is asked for as a generic capability of the compiler (`nuclearlang/`), for every kind.
5. **A project is only `.nuc`.** Everything generated goes to `build/` and is never edited; no target code is
written by hand to make a dialect easier.
6. **The command knows no language.** What it runs for a platform comes from the dialect (`[toolchain]`).
7. **Something new of the tree is written with Synapsis** when one of the three platforms fits it (root rule 9).

- The dialects that implement the platforms are with their language:
`nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/` (`flutter`, `fastapi`, `nestjs`, `react`).
- Runtime packages in the target languages, per platform: Dart (`synapsis`, `synapsis_genkit`), Python
(`synapsis-py`), TypeScript (`synapsis-nest`, `synapsis-web`).
- The framework's commands (`new`, `make`, `gen`, `run`, `test`, `migrate`, `device`...) are commands of `nuclear`:
the module `tools/cli/src/framework/` of the crate `nuclear-cli`. This folder holds no Rust.
- `eval/`: Python scripts.

body: Synapsis is to Nuclear what Actix is to Rust: the language comes with its framework, and no other is needed. It

identical for every dialect of a platform. It has exactly three platforms, `web`, `mobile` and `backend`; a dialect

The framework of NuclearLang, as Actix is Rust's: you write an app, a backend or a web app in Nuclear on one of
three platforms (`mobile`, `backend`, `web`), and a dialect turns it into Flutter, FastAPI, NestJS or React.

rows.title: Synapsis — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - A project holds only its business logic; the transpiler writes injection, JSON, http, state and imports.
- What a target framework lacks comes from a Synapsis runtime package.
- Left out on purpose: a fourth platform, target code in a project, new grammar.

rows.title: Vision — Problem
rows.summary: Writing an app on a platform usually means choosing and wiring many packages: state, JSON, injection, http, routing, translations, tests.
body: Writing an app on a platform usually means choosing and wiring many packages: state, JSON, injection, http,
routing, translations, tests. With Synapsis the dialect already brings that architecture: in Nuclear only the
business logic is written, and constructors, overrides, injection, JSON, http, states, modules and imports are
written by the transpiler.
Synapsis is to Nuclear what Actix is to Rust: the language comes with its framework, and no other is needed. It
is what a project adds to the base language: kinds, decorators, components, `config.nuc`, plugins and tests.
The philosophy is common; each platform applies it its own way, because platforms are incompatible (a `stateless`
view does not exist in an HTTP API). The differences that matter are between a web app, a mobile app and a
backend, not between the languages that run them. So Synapsis has exactly three **platforms** (`web`, `mobile`,
`backend`), each written once in Nuclear, and a **dialect** only changes the language and framework the code comes
out in: the Nuclear code of a project never changes when its dialect changes (ADR-synapsis-0002).

rows.title: Vision — Users
rows.summary: Users
body: | User | Needs |
| AI coding agents | one way to write each thing, the same in every dialect of a platform; a fixed place for each file; diagnostics when the architecture is broken |
| Developers of apps | write business logic only; a project that builds, tests and runs with one command |
| Kind authors (a project, the community) | add a kind to a platform with TOML, templates and a runtime, never touching the compiler |
| Dialect authors | implement a platform in another language and framework from its contract, with the loader saying what is missing |

rows.title: Vision — What it does not do
rows.summary: (ADR-synapsis-0001).
body: - It does not replace the target's own tools: Flutter's CLI still builds and runs; Synapsis drives it.
- It has no fourth platform and no feature that exists in one dialect of a platform only.
- A project holds no target code: everything generated goes to `build/` and is never edited
(ADR-synapsis-0001).
- It never reads target code back into Nuclear (a non-goal of the whole platform).
- It adds nothing to the grammar: a kind is a header and a block of the base language (ADR-synapsis-0004).

rows.title: Kinds, kind packages and plugins — A kind package
rows.summary: kinds/jobs/ ├── kind.toml [package] name, version, platform, description ├── docs.toml the editor documentation of its words ├── fastapi/kind.toml [plugin] (runtime packages, defs, names) + the sections of a dialect and its templates └── nestjs/kind.toml (`Loader::apply_packages`), as a layer…
body: kinds/jobs/
├── kind.toml          [package] name, version, platform, description
├── docs.toml          the editor documentation of its words
├── fastapi/kind.toml  [plugin] (runtime packages, defs, names) + the sections of a dialect and its templates
└── nestjs/kind.toml
- It belongs to one platform. The loader applies only the packages of the dialect's platform
(`Loader::apply_packages`), as a layer named after the package.
- Its implementation for a project is the folder named after the project's dialect, or after a dialect that one
extends. Without one, the package is a gap (`package_gaps`): N0306 when the project enables it.
- A project enables it with `plugins(<name> = true)` in `config.nuc` and keeps its `synapsis(platform, dialect)`.
- The loader looks in `<project>/kinds/` and in the install's `kinds/`. A platform may ship packages in
`platforms/<platform>/kinds/`, which the installer copies; none does today.
- `nuclear kind new <name> -p <platform> -d <dialect>` writes the skeleton in the project; `nuclear add <folder>`
installs a package for every project.

rows.title: Kinds, kind packages and plugins — A plugin
rows.summary: An optional part of a framework that a project carries only when it asks for it.
body: An optional part of a framework that a project carries only when it asks for it.
- A dialect declares it: `[project.plugins.<name>]` with `packages`, `dev_packages`, `defs`, `kinds`, `names`,
`requires`. The names a platform allows are `[platform] plugins` of its contract, the same in every dialect.
- A project enables it: `plugins(genkit = true, googleAI = true)` in `config.nuc`.
- A kind or a name of a plugin that is not enabled is N0304, with the line to add; an unknown plugin or a value
that is not `true` or `false` is N0303.
- The generated manifest lists only the packages of the enabled plugins. The runtimes keep the optional parts in
modules of their own, so a project without a plugin does not need its package.
- Its type definitions are always loaded (their index only), so an editor completes them before the plugin is on.
| Platform | Plugins of its contract |
| `mobile` | `genkit`, `firebaseAI`, `googleAI`, `vertexAI`, `openAI`, `anthropic` |
| `backend` | `sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `redis`, `kafka`, `events`, `ai`, `openai`, `ollama`, `chroma` |
| `web` | none |

rows.title: Kinds, kind packages and plugins — Where a kind comes from
rows.summary: A kind is data: `[kinds.<word>]` plus a template.
body: | Source | Declared in | Who may use it |
| The language's | the language dialect (`dart`'s `data`, `mixin`) | every project of that language |
| Native of a platform | `[platform] kinds` of `platforms/<platform>/platform.toml`, implemented by every dialect of the platform | every project of the platform |
| A kind package | `kinds/<name>/` of a project or of the install | a project of the package's platform that enables it, with a dialect the package implements |
| A project dialect | `<project>/dialects/<name>/` with `extends` | that project, tied to the dialect it extends |
A kind is data: `[kinds.<word>]` plus a template. No kind name is written in Rust. A dialect's own TOML never adds
a kind its platform does not declare (N0305). When a template cannot express something, a generic capability of
the compiler is asked for (an `[options]` entry or a template variable), for every kind.
The loader records the source of every kind in `Dialect.kind_sources` (`KindSource::Language`, `Platform`,
`Package`); the language server shows it in the hover and the completion of a kind (`kind_source` in
`nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp/src/features.rs`).

`nuclear new -p <platform> -d <dialect> <name>` creates it; without `-d` it gets the platform's
`default_dialect`. The code lives in `components/<c>/` by layer, with `config/`, `shared/` and `test/` beside them;
the place of each kind's file is the platform's `[layout]`. Everything generated goes to `build/` and is never
edited. `nuclear.toml` is for projects of a language dialect without Synapsis.
What every project looks like, and why, is in [rules.md](rules.md).

rows.title: Architecture — From `.nuc` to a running app
rows.summary: 1. The loader (`nuclear-dialect`) loads the project's dialect: the chain language dialect → framework dialect (→ project dialect), then the platform's contract, then the kind packages of that platform.
body: 1. The loader (`nuclear-dialect`) loads the project's dialect: the chain language dialect → framework dialect (→
project dialect), then the platform's contract, then the kind packages of that platform. A dialect that leaves
its contract is refused (`platforms/docs/02-architecture/contract.md`).
2. The transpiler (`nuclear-transpile::project`) reads `config.nuc`, generates `contracts/<name>/` when the project
declares contracts ([shared-contracts.md](shared-contracts.md)), checks the architecture rules of the dialect
(N0301, N0302) and writes the target project into `build/` with the dialect's templates.
3. The `nuclear` command runs what the dialect's `[toolchain]` declares in the generated project: install, run,
test, migrate, add a package. It uses `nuclear-transpile::project` and `nuclear-dialect::Loader` as a library
and knows no language (its mobile path still calls Flutter directly: [rules.md](rules.md), rule 9).
4. The generated code imports the platform's runtime package, which the generated manifest adds by itself; a
project lists only third-party packages and plugins in `config.nuc`.

rows.title: The rules every platform and dialect follows
rows.summary: 1. Light clean architecture.
body: 1. **Light clean architecture.** Components with layers (`config`, `data`, `domain`, and the platform's entry
layer: `presentation` in mobile and web, `api` in backend) and a facade (`appcomponent`). The layers exist in
the generated code, not as ceremony in Nuclear (ADR-dart-0001, ADR-synapsis-0003).
2. **Closed components.** From another component only its public kinds are visible (the facade, models, events,
global components, guards, screens); the transpiler checks it (N0302). Who calls whom is checked too (N0301): a
use case only from the facade; a service only from a use case or an aggregate (ADR-synapsis-0003). The rules
are data of each dialect: `[architecture]` (`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md` §4).
3. **Injection by header.** A typed parameter in a kind's header is injected (ADR-synapsis-0003).
4. **Errors as values.** Use cases return `Result<E, T>` (ADR-lang-0006, ADR-lang-0006); the runtime's errors carry
an HTTP status in backend.
5. **Only `.nuc` in the project.** Everything generated goes to `build/` and is never edited (ADR-synapsis-0001).
6. **Only third-party packages and plugins in `config.nuc`.** The framework's packages are added automatically
(ADR-mobile-0001), a plugin's packages only when it is enabled (ADR-synapsis-0004).

rows.title: The rules every platform and dialect follows
rows.summary: Nuclear.
body: - **The platform names no dialect** (rule 11). A platform's reference, docs, examples and diagnostics hold only
Nuclear. The standard library is Nuclear's own (`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/library.md`, ADR-lang-0009): a
target's library name (`push`, `len`, `toUpperCase`) in platform code, references, docs or examples is a bug.
- **Nuclear and Synapsis first** (rule 12). A new development of the tree (a service, a tool, an agent) is a
Synapsis project when one of the three platforms fits.

body: `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name>` writes, for any platform, the models, the repository (REST over an `Http`
connection or a database), one use case per action, the component's facade, the controller (backend) or the screen
with its state manager (mobile, web) and their tests; everything compiles as written. The fields come from
`--fields "id:int name:string"`, from an answer (`--from-json <url|file>`: nested models and pages included, `@key`
for snake_case keys) or from a spec (`--from-spec spec.md`: its example answer, its `Key | Type` table, its
`GET <url>` line). `nuclear gen inspect` lists what the project has; nothing is ever overwritten.
`nuclear gen usecase <component> <Name>` wires a use case into its component: its alias in the facade and, on the
backend, `--route "POST orders/{id}/cancel"` adds its route to the controller of `orders` (made when missing). A use
case with rules of its own is written first and then wired, with the signature the project gives it; one that only
calls a repository method is written by the command too: `--calls OrderRepository.pending`.
Every option, what each platform gets, the refusals and worked examples: [Generators](generators.md). The MCP server
gives the same tools to an agent, and the editor's Builder runs them before planning. Why: ADR-codegen-0001.

rows.title: Synapsis: three platforms, one code per platform — Mobile: the backend's ORM on the device
rows.summary: A mobile app keeps what it fetches with two words (ADR-mobile-0006).
body: A mobile app keeps what it fetches with two words (ADR-mobile-0006). `@primary` on a field gives the model an encrypted
local table (`@entity("characters")` names it; the same database on phones, desktops and web); `saveLocal = true` on the repository makes every GET that answers that model save its rows and get a
twin `<method>AsLocal()`, same signature, that answers the last rows from the device without a request. The
queries are the backend repository's: `where`, `orderBy`, `limit`, `offset`, `getOne`, `getMany`, `count`,
`exists`, `update`, `delete`, plus `find`, `findAll`, `save`, `remove`.
```nuclear
@entity("characters")
Character
@primary
id: int
name: string
status: string
@repository(path = "character", saveLocal = true)
repository CharacterRepository
@get(path = ":id")
getOne(id: int) Result<CharacterError, Character>     // + getOneAsLocal(id)
alive() Character[]
~local<Character>().where({ "status": "Alive" }).orderBy("name").getMany()
Encryption (AES-256, key in the device's secure storage) is on by default and is a line of the config files:
`local: LocalDatabase = LocalDatabase(encrypted = true)` in the project's `appConfig`, or in a component's `config`
for its own tables.

rows.summary: The platforms share the same architecture, so moving from one to another means learning its kinds, not a new way to think: use cases) and its entry points (`presentation/` in Flutter, `api/` in the backends, `ai/` for agents).
body: The platforms share the same architecture, so moving from one to another means learning its kinds, not a new
way to think:
- **Components** by feature (`components/tasks/`), each with `data/` (entities, repositories), `domain/` (models,
use cases) and its entry points (`presentation/` in Flutter, `api/` in the backends, `ai/` for agents).
- **Kinds** say what a declaration is: `usecase`, `repository`, `controller`, `stateless`, `agent`, `graph`...
The dialect writes the class, its decorators, its registration in the injector and its imports.
- **`appcomponent`** is what the rest of the app sees of a component; one component never reaches inside another.
- **Errors are values:** a use case answers `Result<Error, T>`; a controller turns `Err(NotFound(...))` into a 404.
- **Connections** (a database, a chat model, Kafka, Redis, an AI provider) are listed in
`config/project_config.nuc`, never opened by hand.
- **Tests in Nuclear:** `tests Name` with `@test(...)` methods, written for the target's test runner.

rows.summary: The optional parts of each framework are plugins, enabled in the project's `config.nuc`.
body: The optional parts of each framework are **plugins**, enabled in the project's `config.nuc`. A project without a
plugin does not carry its packages:
```nuclear
// config.nuc
plugins(genkit = true, googleAI = true)
| Dialect | Plugins |
| `flutter` | `genkit`, and its providers `firebaseAI`, `googleAI`, `vertexAI`, `openAI`, `anthropic` |
| `fastapi`, `nestjs` (the backend platform: the same list) | `sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `redis`, `kafka`, `events`, `ai`, `openai`, `ollama`, `chroma` |
- Only the enabled plugins reach `pubspec.yaml`, `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`. Turning one off removes its
packages on the next build.
- A provider plugin enables the plugin it needs (`googleAI` enables `genkit`; `ollama` enables `ai`).
- Using a kind or a class of a plugin that is not enabled is diagnostic **N0304**, which says which line to add.
The editor still completes those names, so you can discover them.
How a dialect declares its plugins: [projects.md §3.3](../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md). Why: ADR-synapsis-0004.
The native kinds of each platform, and how to write your own kind without touching the compiler: [Kinds](kinds.md).

rows.title: Synapsis: three platforms, one code per platform — Real time, guards and a host page: configuration
rows.summary: Real time is configured, not written (ADR-synapsis-0008).
body: Real time is configured, not written (ADR-synapsis-0008). A backend with `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` in its
connections (plugin `websocket`) serves its same controllers over a WebSocket, and `~publish("topic", value)` reaches
the clients subscribed to the topic. A web app with `WebSocket(url = "ws://localhost:8000/ws")` instead of `Http(...)`
sends its repositories' calls over it, unchanged; a repository method `@on("topic")` that returns `Stream<T>` is what
the server pushes, and a state manager follows it with `listen(stream, (value) => ...)`.
A backend's `guards: Guard[] = [NoOrigin(), Token(value = env("TOKEN"))]` checks the headers of every request, over
both transports; `@controller("x", guards = [...])` adds a controller's own (ADR-synapsis-0007). A web app also builds
as a bundle that mounts in another page, `mount(element, { bridge, path })`, in a shadow root with the host's CSS
variables, and sends its calls through the host's bridge (ADR-synapsis-0009).
```sh
nuclear new chat_api -p backend --websocket --token CHAT_TOKEN   # the WebSocket and the guards in its config
nuclear new chat_ui -p web --websocket                           # a WebSocket connection instead of Http

rows.summary: What a resource is made of on each platform:
body: | Option | Meaning |
| `--source rest:<base url>` \| `rest` \| `db` | where the data lives: another API (an HTTP repository) or the database (backend only). Default: `db`, or `rest` when a url was given |
| `--actions list,get,search,create,update,delete` | one use case each. Default: `list,get` for an API, every one for a database |

rows.summary: // Cancels an order that is still pending; Conflict (409) when it is not.
body: ```nuclear
// Cancels an order that is still pending; Conflict (409) when it is not.
usecase CancelOrder(repository: OrderRepository)
exec(id: int) Result<Error, Order>
found = ~repository.find(id)
if found.status != "pending"
return Err(Conflict("only a pending order is cancelled"))
found.status = "cancelled"
Ok(~repository.save(found))
```sh
nuclear gen usecase orders CancelOrder --route "POST orders/{id}/cancel"
It adds the alias to the facade and the route to the controller, with the signature `exec` has in the project:
```nuclear
appcomponent OrdersAppComponent
cancelOrder() = CancelOrder.exec
```nuclear
@controller("orders")
controller OrdersController(app: OrdersAppComponent)
@post("{id}/cancel")
cancelOrder(id: int) Result<Error, Order>
~app.cancelOrder(id)
`--route "<VERB> <prefix>[/<path>]"` is backend only. The first segment is the controller's prefix: `orders` is
`OrdersController`, created when the component has none. A `{name}` of the path is a parameter of the use case; the
other parameters arrive as the verb sends them. The route calls the use case with `~` only when its `exec` awaits.
On mobile and web the command adds the alias (and, with `--calls`, writes the use case). What a screen shows of it,
a method of its state manager and the state it emits, is written by hand.

**A use case that only calls a repository method** is written by the command, because there is nothing to decide:
```sh
nuclear gen usecase orders PageOrders --calls OrderRepository.page --route "GET orders/pages/{page}"

The parameters and the answer are the method's own, read from the project. An answer that is not a `Result` goes

rows.title: Generators: the standard code, written by a command — 3. What every generator keeps
rows.summary: members they lack, each one whole (a route with its decorator and its body).
body: - **Nothing is overwritten.** A file that exists is kept. The facade, the repository and the controller get only the
members they lack, each one whole (a route with its decorator and its body). So an action added to a resource that
exists (`nuclear gen resource orders Order ... --actions list,get,search` on one that had `list,get`) adds its use
case, its alias, the repository's method and its route, and what is written still compiles. Running a command twice changes nothing: the second
time every file says `kept`.
- **Nothing is declared twice.** A name another file of the project declares stops the command before it writes.
- **Nothing is left to fill in.** What a command writes compiles as written. When it cannot write something finished,
it refuses and says what to do.

rows.title: Generators: the standard code, written by a command — 4. When a generator refuses
rows.summary: 4. When a generator refuses
body: | It says | What to do |

| `<Name> is not declared. A use case with rules of its own is written first ...` | write the use case in the file it names, then run the command again; or give `--calls` when it only calls a repository |
| the repository, or its method, is not declared | `--calls` names a method a repository of the project has: `nuclear gen inspect` lists the repositories and their files |
| a `{name}` of the route is not a parameter of the use case | name the path's parameter like the one `exec` takes |
| the use case belongs to another component | give the component that declares it |
| the platform has no routes | `--route` is backend only: on mobile and web leave it out |
| a type of `--fields` is not declared | declare the model first, or take the fields from an answer (`--from-json`), which writes the nested models too |
| the name is declared in another file | pick another name, or remove the old declaration when it is a leftover |

| a database resource has no generated search | which column is searched is yours to say: write the query in the repository, then `nuclear gen usecase <component> Search<Names> --calls <Name>Repository.<method>` |

rows.summary: Anything a project repeats can become a kind: a scheduled job, a webhook handler, a report, a screen layout your app uses forty times.
body: Anything a project repeats can become a kind: a scheduled job, a webhook handler, a report, a screen layout your
app uses forty times. An extension kind is a **package**: its TOML, templates, the runtime it needs in the target
language, its type definitions and its editor docs, with one implementation per dialect it supports. It is enabled
like a plugin, `plugins(jobs = true)`, and the project keeps `synapsis(platform = "backend", dialect = "fastapi")`.
A package belongs to one platform: a backend package never shows up in a mobile project, even when the word exists
there with another meaning (`repository` is table queries in backend and HTTP calls in mobile).
**The editor knows the difference.** Completion lists only the kinds of your platform: the native ones plus the
packages your `config.nuc` enables. Hover says where a kind comes from (the platform, or a package and the dialects
it implements) and shows its docs. A kind of a package made for another platform, or not implemented for your
dialect, is reported with the line to fix.
The rule of portability (ADR-synapsis-0002, ADR-synapsis-0004): the Nuclear you write with a kind is the same in every dialect that
implements it. A package implemented for one dialect only ties your project to that dialect, exactly as using a
dialect's type definitions does; the compiler tells you which dialects you can still build with.

`fields`, `methods`, `methods_code`, `members`, `decor` (each decorator with its arguments), `ret_info`, `extends`,
`implements`, `generics`, `file`, `component`, `kind`, and more ([projects.md §5](../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md)). Templates

rows.title: Kinds: the libraries of Synapsis — 4. What a kind cannot do
rows.summary: read.
body: - **Add syntax.** Inside the block you write Nuclear; the kind chooses what the block becomes, never how Nuclear is
read. If something needs new grammar, it is not a kind.
- **Touch the compiler.** If a template cannot express what you need, ask for a generic capability (a template
variable or an `[options]` entry): it is added for every kind, never as a special case. Do not fake the output.
- **Offer a second way of writing the same thing.** A kind exists only if it removes repeated code of the target
(golden rule, ADR-lang-0001).
- **Generate code an expert would not write:** no reflection, no unused layers, no analyzer warnings.
- **Change with the dialect.** The Nuclear of a kind is the same in every dialect that implements it.
Rules and format: [dialects.md](../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md) §5.4, §7 and §8, [projects.md](../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md) §5.
Why: ADR-synapsis-0002, ADR-synapsis-0004.

rows.title: Kinds: the libraries of Synapsis
rows.summary: A kind is the word before the name of a declaration: `usecase CreateTask`, `controller TasksController`, `stateless Home`.
body: A **kind** is the word before the name of a declaration: `usecase CreateTask`, `controller TasksController`,
`stateless Home`. It tells Synapsis what that block is, and the dialect writes the whole declaration in the target
(the class, its base, its imports, its boilerplate) so you only write the logic. Kinds are to Synapsis what
libraries are to a language: a platform comes with its **native kinds**, and a project or the community can add
**extension kinds** on top of a dialect, without touching the compiler (ADR-synapsis-0004).
The parser never knows a kind. Every kind is "a header and a block" of the base grammar; the kind itself is data:
a TOML entry and a template. That is why adding one needs no lexer, no parser and no Rust.

body: - **Debugging in Nuclear:** a breakpoint in a `.nuc` stops the app on that line (with Debug), the pause

accordion of bars; a click on a name opens its `.nuc` at the line. Without `--monitor` nothing is measured.

rows.title: Nuclear's helpers of lodash — Rules
rows.summary: 1. lodash is adapted to Nuclear, never Nuclear to lodash (the user, 2026-11-21).
body: 1. **lodash is adapted to Nuclear, never Nuclear to lodash** (the user, 2026-11-21). A function is here when it
serves Nuclear code; one that only makes sense in JavaScript (the `arguments` object, prototypes, type coercion,
a class compared with another, a `this` binding) is not written.
2. **What the language's library has is not repeated**: `map`, `filter`, `find`, `take`, `unique`, `groupBy`,
`trim`... are members of Nuclear's types (`nuclear help library`). `docs/07-reference/functions.md` says which
member each lodash name is.
3. **Typed.** A helper names its parameters and their types; an iteratee is a lambda, never a text or a pattern
object; several lists are given as their own parameters, since Nuclear has no rest parameter. Only the helpers
of paths (`get`, `set`, `has`, `unset`, `merge`, `cloneDeep`) take `any`, over maps and lists.
4. **The same in every dialect.** A case is done when it prints the same in TypeScript, Dart and Python with no
warning of the target's checker. A difference between the targets is a bug of the compiler or of a dialect:
it is fixed there (`nuclearlang/`), with its test, never worked around here.
5. **A case states what it wants** (`check(name, got, want)`), taken from lodash's own tests and documentation
where they apply. A random helper takes its source of numbers as a parameter, so its cases are fixed.

**What it is.** 117 helpers of [lodash](https://lodash.com) over lists, maps, texts, numbers and functions
(`chunk`, `difference`, `uniqBy`, `partition`, `orderBy`, `camelCase`, `pick`, `get`, `merge`, `memoize`...), written
once in Nuclear. They are part of the language: a program calls them with no `use`, and the transpiler writes only
the ones it calls, in every dialect.
**Why it exists.** Two reasons. A Nuclear program gets the helpers every program ends up writing, the same in every
dialect. And the compiler gets a real library to prove itself on: writing it found more than a dozen places where the same Nuclear
gave another result, or no program at all, in one of the targets; each is fixed in the compiler with its test. It
leaves out on purpose what Nuclear's own library already has and what only means something in JavaScript.
**How we made it.** lodash's behaviour, not its code: each function is written in Nuclear with typed parameters,
and its cases come from lodash's tests and documentation where they apply to Nuclear (226 cases). lodash is
MIT-licensed work of the OpenJS Foundation and its contributors; this library copies none of its source.
**Try it.**

body: - **`words`** splits on what is not a letter or a digit and where a lower-case letter meets an upper-case one; it
does not split a run of capitals (`XMLHttp`) nor letters from digits (`foo2bar`), as lodash does.

rows.title: The functions — What is written another way
rows.summary: (`first`, `second`).
body: - **Pairs.** Nuclear has no tuples: `zip`, `unzip`, `partition`, `toPairs` and `fromPairs` use `Pair<A, B>`
(`first`, `second`).
- **Several lists.** No rest parameter: `difference`, `union`, `intersection`, `xor` and `zip` take two lists; more
are chained.
- **Keys are texts.** `countBy`, `keyBy`, `uniqBy`, `differenceBy`... take a `key` lambda that gives a `string`.
- **Random helpers** (`sample`, `sampleSize`, `shuffle`, `randomInt`) take the source of numbers (`Math.random`
or a fixed one): a program chooses whether it can be repeated.
- **Names changed** because the lodash name is a member of Nuclear's library with another meaning or the helper
differs: `roundTo`, `floorTo`, `ceilTo` (`round`, `floor`, `ceil` with a precision), `randomInt` (`random`),
`trimChars`, `trimCharsStart`, `trimCharsEnd` (`trim` with characters), `uniqueIds` (`uniqueId`, as a maker with
its own count instead of a count of the whole program), `forEachIndexed` (`forEach` with the index),
`orderBy(xs, keys, descending)` (a flag per key instead of `"asc"` / `"desc"`).
- **Functions of fixed parameters.** `partial`, `partialRight`, `flip` and `curry` are for a function of two
parameters, `memoize` and `negate` for one, `once`, `after` and `before` for none: a function of any number of
parameters has no type in Nuclear.

rows.title: The platforms of Synapsis — Rules
rows.summary: 1. A platform is written in Nuclear only.
body: 1. **A platform is written in Nuclear only.** Its contract, its reference, its brief, its examples and its
diagnostics name no dialect, no language and no target's library.
2. **Exactly three platforms.** A new one is a decision of the user and a new ADR of the framework.
3. **The contract comes first.** A kind, a decorator or a plugin is declared in `platform.toml` and implemented by
every dialect of the platform in the same change; the loader refuses a dialect that leaves the contract
(N0305). Only a plugin may be brought later by a dialect (a warning).
4. **No name of a kind or of a decorator is written in Rust.** A rule every dialect shares is data of the contract
(`[decorators.args]`, `[decorators.fields]`, `[layout]`).
5. **What only some projects need is not in a contract:** it is a kind package or a plugin
(`../docs/02-architecture/kinds-and-plugins.md`).
6. **One fact, one platform.** This level describes no platform: it links to it. A platform does not repeat what
is here.
7. A file under a platform's `docs/07-reference/` or `docs/08-guides/` is normative and shipped by the installer:
it changes only with the feature it describes.

rows.title: The platforms of Synapsis — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - What matters is phone, API or browser, not the language underneath.
- A fixed contract keeps the Nuclear of one dialect compatible with another.
- Left out on purpose: a fourth platform, any dialect's name in a contract.

rows.title: The contract of a platform: `platform.toml` — Changing a contract
rows.summary: 1. A new kind, decorator or plugin is written in `[platform]` first; a kind also gets its `[layout]` path (a test requires one for every kind) and, where the platform has them, a `[skeletons]` entry in its `generators.toml`.
body: 1. A new kind, decorator or plugin is written in `[platform]` first; a kind also gets its `[layout]` path (a test
requires one for every kind) and, where the platform has them, a `[skeletons]` entry in its `generators.toml`.
2. Every dialect of the platform implements it in the same change, or the loader refuses the dialect that does
not. A plugin is the one thing a dialect may bring later (a warning).
3. Every new word gets its editor documentation in the dialect's `docs.toml` (a test requires it), and the
platform's reference (`<platform>/docs/07-reference/<platform>.md`) gets the rule, in Nuclear only.
4. The examples and their goldens follow: [testing.md](../05-standards/testing.md).
A kind that only one project or one community needs is not added to a contract: it is a kind package
(`nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/02-architecture/kinds-and-plugins.md`).

rows.title: The contract of a platform: `platform.toml` — How a dialect implements it
rows.summary: A framework dialect is a folder `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/` (`dialect.toml`, `docs.toml`, `templates/`).
body: A framework dialect is a folder `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/` (`dialect.toml`,
`docs.toml`, `templates/`). Its `[dialect]` table names the language dialect it extends and its platform:
It then gives each kind of the contract a `[kinds.<word>]` with its template, lists the decorators its templates
read (`[decorators] consumed`), declares the platform's plugins (`[project.plugins.<name>]`), the architecture
rules (`[architecture]`) and what the `nuclear` command runs (`[toolchain]`). A project dialect that extends it
inherits the platform.

rows.title: The contract of a platform: `platform.toml` — Sections
rows.summary: `decorators` is the list of the `@words` a project may write: one in lower case that is not in it is N0309 in a project of the platform.
body: | Section | Holds | Read by |

| `[platform]` | `name` (must be the folder's and the one the dialect names), `description`, `default_dialect` (what `nuclear new -p <platform>` uses without `-d`), `kinds`, `decorators`, `plugins` | the loader's check (below) |
| `[decorators.args]` | decorator → its named arguments (`!` = required), the same in every dialect; a dialect's own entry wins | N0217 |
| `[decorators.fields]` | decorator → the rule a field with it must meet: `optional`, `list`, `target`, `sibling`, `inverse`, `with` | N0308 |
| `[decorators.replaced]` | a removed decorator → what replaces it | N0309 |
| `[layout]` | kind → the path of its file, with `{component}`, `{screen}` and `{file}` (the name in snake_case) | `nuclear help layout --dialect <d>`, `nuclear make`, `nuclear gen`, agents |
`decorators` is the list of the `@words` a project may write: one in lower case that is not in it is N0309 in a
project of the platform. The web contract has no `[decorators.*]` tables.

rows.title: The contract of a platform: `platform.toml`
rows.summary: `<platform>/platform.toml` says what every dialect of the platform must implement, identically.
body: `<platform>/platform.toml` says what every dialect of the platform must implement, identically. It is data read by
the compiler's loader; nothing in it names a language. The normative description of each key, with the values a
generator template gets, is `nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md` §1. Paths that start with `nuclearlang/`
or `tools/` start at the root of the tree.

rows.title: The contract of a platform: `platform.toml` — What the code generator writes: not in the contract
rows.summary: What `nuclear make` and `nuclear gen` write for a platform is the code generator's, in `tools/code_generator/platforms/<platform>/generators.toml` (`tools/code_generator/AGENTS.md`).
body: What `nuclear make` and `nuclear gen` write for a platform is the code generator's, in
`tools/code_generator/platforms/<platform>/generators.toml` (`tools/code_generator/AGENTS.md`). The loader reads it
with the contract (`Loader::generators_file`, from `Home.generators`; `<install>/generators/` in an install):
| Section | Holds | Read by |
| `[skeletons]` | kind → the smallest file of the kind that compiles, with `{{Name}}`, `{{name}}`, `{{component}}`, `{{Component}}`, `{{table}}` | `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` |
| `[gen]` | how a generator writes an `Http` connection (`http`, `http_named`) | `nuclear gen` |
| `[[generators.<what>]]` | the files `nuclear gen <what>` writes (`component`, `resource`, `usecase`), in order: `kind`, `name`, `template`, and `when`, `each`, `merge` | `nuclear gen` |
The mobile file has no `[skeletons]`.

rows.title: The contract of a platform: `platform.toml` — What the loader checks
rows.summary: `check_platform` in `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-dialect/src/model.rs` runs when a dialect that names a platform is loaded.
body: `check_platform` in `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-dialect/src/model.rs` runs when a dialect that names a platform is
loaded. Every finding is the diagnostic N0305; an error means the dialect does not load.
| Case | Result |
| The dialect names a platform without a `platform.toml` in the loader's platform folders | error |
| The file is not valid TOML, has no `[platform]`, or its `name` is not the platform the dialect names | error |
| The dialect misses a kind of `kinds` | error |
| The dialect adds a kind that is not in `kinds` (the language dialect's own kinds, such as `dart`'s `mixin`, do not count) | error |
| The dialect consumes a decorator that is not in `decorators` | error |
| The dialect declares a plugin that is not in `plugins` | error |
| `[layout]` names something that is not a kind of the platform | error |

| `[skeletons]` or a `[[generators.<what>]]` of the platform's `generators.toml` names a kind with no place in `[layout]`; a generator's `name` or `template` does not compile (`load_generators`, same file) | error |
| The dialect does not bring a plugin of `plugins` yet | warning |

rows.title: The contract of a platform: `platform.toml` — What the loader checks
rows.summary: The loader also copies the platform's data into the loaded dialect, so every tool reads it from one place: `platform_decorators`, `decorator_args`, `decorator_fields`, `replaced_decorators`, `layout` from the contract; `skeletons`, `generators`, `gen_values` from the generators file.
body: The loader also copies the platform's data into the loaded dialect, so every tool reads it from one place:
`platform_decorators`, `decorator_args`, `decorator_fields`, `replaced_decorators`, `layout` from the contract;
`skeletons`, `generators`, `gen_values` from the generators file.
The contract is found by `Loader::platform_file`: the first `<platform>/platform.toml` of `Loader.platform_paths`,
which are the `platforms/` folder next to each dialects folder and the `platforms` of each home (the install, then
the source tree). The generators file is found the same way by `Loader::generators_file`: the first
`<platform>/generators.toml` of `Loader.generator_paths`.

rows.title: What a platform is — In an install
rows.summary: `installer/release/stage.sh` copies, for each platform: `platform.toml`, `docs/07-reference/` and `docs/08-guides/` into `$NUCLEAR_HOME/platforms/<platform>/`, every folder of `packages/` into `$NUCLEAR_HOME/packages/`, and `kinds/` into `$NUCLEAR_HOME/kinds/`.
body: `installer/release/stage.sh` copies, for each platform: `platform.toml`, `docs/07-reference/` and `docs/08-guides/`
into `$NUCLEAR_HOME/platforms/<platform>/`, every folder of `packages/` into `$NUCLEAR_HOME/packages/`, and
`kinds/` into `$NUCLEAR_HOME/kinds/`. A built JavaScript package must have its `dist/` or the staging stops. What a

The loader finds the contracts in its platform folders (`Loader.platform_paths`): the `platforms/` of the install
and, while the source tree is on disk, `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/` (`nuclear_dialect::Home`).
The generators of each platform are not in a platform folder: the install has them in `$NUCLEAR_HOME/generators/`,
copied from `tools/code_generator/platforms/` (`Home.generators`, `Loader::generators_file`).

rows.title: What a platform is — What a platform folder holds
rows.summary: ├── platform.toml the contract every dialect of the platform implements (contract.md) ├── packages/ the runtime packages: what the target frameworks lack, in the target languages ├── examples/ projects in Nuclear, and expected/ with their golden output ├── checks/ scripts that run the generated…
body: <platform>/
├── platform.toml     the contract every dialect of the platform implements (contract.md)
├── packages/         the runtime packages: what the target frameworks lack, in the target languages
├── examples/         projects in Nuclear, and expected/ with their golden output
├── checks/           scripts that run the generated code against the target's own tools
├── kinds/            kind packages shipped with the platform (optional; none today)
├── docs/             its documents; 07-reference/ is the normative text, 08-guides/ what a user reads
└── AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, README.md, CHANGELOG.md
What is **not** here: the dialects that implement the platform and the type definitions of its runtime packages,
which live with their language (`nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/`,
`nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/defs/<package>/<version>/`), and what `nuclear make` and `nuclear gen` write, which
is the code generator's (`tools/code_generator/platforms/<platform>/generators.toml`).

rows.title: What a platform is — What a platform folder holds
rows.summary: project gets them by itself; a project never lists them in `config.nuc`.
body: - **Runtime packages.** One per target language of the platform's dialects, plus those of its plugins. A generated
project gets them by itself; a project never lists them in `config.nuc`. A change to the public API of a runtime
package means regenerating its type definitions (the platform's own documents say how).
- **Examples.** Each platform has the complete projects its tests build; `examples/expected/<project>/` is the
golden output, compared by `cargo test` and accepted with `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test`.
- **Checks.** What `cargo test` cannot do: the target's analyzer, the target's test runner and a live run of the
generated project ([testing.md](../05-standards/testing.md)).
- **Reference.** `docs/07-reference/<platform>.md` is the platform's rules in Nuclear only, and
`docs/07-reference/brief/<platform>.md` the short sheet an agent reads. How a dialect writes each kind is in that
dialect's reference, `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/docs/07-reference/<dialect>.md`.

rows.summary: Paths without a root are relative to `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/`; a path that starts with `nuclearlang/`, `installer/` or `.github/` starts at the root of the tree.
body: Paths without a root are relative to `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/`; a path that starts with
`nuclearlang/`, `installer/` or `.github/` starts at the root of the tree.
A platform is a specification written in Nuclear only: the project layout, `config.nuc`, the kinds, the
decorators, the connections, the plugins, the tests and the errors of one kind of software. It names no language.
It is what the user and the agent write; a dialect is only the language and framework the code comes out in, and

| [`backend`](../../backend/AGENTS.md) | HTTP APIs, data, events and AI agents | `fastapi` | `python/frameworks/fastapi`, `typescript/frameworks/nestjs` | `synapsis-py` (Python), `synapsis-nest` (TypeScript) |

rows.title: What a platform is
rows.summary: Kinds and features may differ between platforms (`stateless` is mobile and web, `controller` is backend), never between the dialects of one platform.
body: Kinds and features may differ between platforms (`stateless` is mobile and web, `controller` is backend), never
between the dialects of one platform. The same word may mean different things in two platforms: `repository` is
table queries in backend and HTTP calls in mobile. The web platform takes the kinds of the mobile platform that
make sense in a browser, with the same words, so an app's domain reads the same on a phone and on the web
(ADR-web-0001).

rows.title: Testing a platform — Conventions
rows.summary: them; the test only rewrites `dialect = "..."` in its `config.nuc`.
body: - **A conformance example is the platform's Nuclear**, with nothing tied to one dialect, so it builds with all of
them; the test only rewrites `dialect = "..."` in its `config.nuc`.
- **Each dialect's output passes its own strict check:** `tsc --strict`, `pyright --strict`, `flutter analyze`
with `flutter_lints`, the tests written in Nuclear, and a smoke run.
- **A platform with one dialect** (`mobile`, `web` today) has no conformance test yet: it gets one with its second
dialect.
- **An example is a golden.** A change in generated output is accepted with `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test` and
reviewed as a diff, never edited by hand.
